$comment: The recorded state of the `endora new storefront` acceptance criterion
(specs/071-modular-packaging/roadmap.md § F7). `acceptance:storefront-scaffold:ci`
compares a run to this file and fails on drift in EITHER direction: a newly-red
assertion fails, and so does a newly-green one nobody recorded. An unrecorded pass
is a criterion whose meaning moved without anybody reading it.
It landed all-green, which is unusual for an acceptance file in this repository and
is the finding rather than a formality: `acceptance:package-schema` landed red on
seven of nine because the capability it measures did not exist yet, and this one
measures a capability that turned out to be one manifest line short of working.
The roadmap named this criterion as the half that `could not be sized without
trying it` — whether a scaffolded storefront builds from packed tarballs depends on
how much of the packages' `exports` maps and `use client` boundaries survive an
install that is not a workspace link. Measured: all of it. The one thing that did
not survive was the reference storefront's own manifest, which declared none of the
eight `@tiptap/*` packages its build resolves from the workspace root.
A6 is `pass` because the job boots a backend for it. A run with no
PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL records `unmeasured` instead — never a pass — because a boot
with no backend measures the storefront's error page rather than the storefront.
If this job ever stops booting one, A6 drifts to `unmeasured` and fails, which is
the direction that keeps the headline claim honest.
SINCE 2026-09-06 THE RUN SUPPLIES THE INPUTS THE COMMAND REQUIRES, AND THE SIX
STATES BELOW ARE UNCHANGED BECAUSE OF IT RATHER THAN IN SPITE OF IT. Feature 117
removed the storefront's invented defaults and gave `endora new storefront` a
four-tier input resolution ending in a refusal. This criterion had been invoking
it with no inputs at all — correct only while the defaults existed — so from the
moment they went the command refused, the run exited 2, and all six assertions
were unrun. That is the state this record exists to refuse, and no comparison
against it could see it: a run that cannot measure never reaches the comparison.
It supplies them as flags, which is tier 1, and the choice is deliberate: the
copy's `.env` is what the command now writes and what `next build` and `next
start` read, so a harness that pre-placed that file — tier 2, which the command
also supports — would be supplying an artefact whose production is part of what
A5 and A6 measure. Which inputs, and what value each gets, is derived: the
population is `storefront/environment-inputs.mjs`, the values are
`storefront/.env.example`, and a required input neither reaches is a refusal
rather than a value the harness makes up. One is: `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` is
declared required and is supplied by nothing in this tree — not `.env.example`,
not the Dockerfile's build arguments, not `build:storefront`, not
`compose.prod.yml` — so it carries a stand-in whose value is the storefront's own
fallback, and the entry retires the day any derivation reaches it.
SINCE 2026-09-06 A6 IS TWO BOOTS AND ITS `pass` MEANS MORE THAN IT DID. The state
is unchanged and the claim behind it is not: the run now points the instance at the
backend through the variables the instance's own `.env.example` declares, and then
boots it a second time with those same variables aimed at an address nothing listens
on. A pass needs the first boot below 500 and the second at or above it. Until this
landed the harness exported `PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` — the *backend's* variable, for the
public origin its gateway callbacks need, and one no file in the storefront has ever
read — so the instance fell back to the `http://localhost:3001` its fetchers compile
in. A6 was therefore green whenever the run's backend happened to sit on that address
and red whenever it sat anywhere else, in both cases for a reason belonging to the
harness rather than to the criterion. The probe is what stops the green meaning `the
fallback answered`: a second boot whose configuration reaches nothing has to fail, or
the first answer proves nothing and the assertion is `unmeasured`.
SINCE 2026-09-04 THE RECORD IS PER SUPPLY ROUTE (feature 104, § 1.6). The six
assertions are the same under both; what differs is how the instance got its
`@endora-commerce/*` packages, and `A3 pass` therefore means two different things.
`tarball` packs them out of this checkout and pins them through `pnpm.overrides`;
`registry` installs the semver ranges the scaffold wrote, from a real registry,
through the `.npmrc` `endora new storefront --registry` emits. The mode is chosen
by ENDORA_NPM_REGISTRY in the environment, so a run with no registry variables —
every local run, and the CI job as it stands — takes the tarball route.
`registry` is recorded `unrun`, and that is a state rather than a placeholder — but
its reason has changed and the old one was measurably false by 2026-09-06. It read
`no version of the three packages is on the rehearsal registry ... every manifest
still reads 0.0.0`, and that stopped being true when they published at `0.7.0`: job
43527, on master at 1d906d15a, took the registry route and reported `A3 PASS — pnpm
install succeeded outside the checkout, resolving 3 published ranges`. The mode runs,
and it runs on every master pipeline, because ENDORA_NPM_REGISTRY is protected and a
merge-request pipeline resolves it to nothing. What is still true is the refusal:
recording seven predicted states is the one thing this file exists to refuse, and the
one measured run of the route measured the environment defect the 2026-09-07 entry
below removes — so its A5 and A6 are states of the harness rather than of the
criterion, and writing them here would record a claim that a scaffolded storefront is
*expected* not to build. This machine cannot make an honest run of it either: the
registry and its token are protected CI variables and `projects/:id/variables` answers
403. So the record arrives, as it always would have, from the first real run — the
master pipeline of the merge that lands the repair — which drifts and names every
state it measured.
SINCE 2026-09-06 THERE IS AN A7, AND IT IS THE ONLY ASSERTION IN THIS FILE THAT
READS THE PAGE RATHER THAN THE STATUS LINE. `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` was declared
required by `storefront/environment-inputs.mjs` and supplied by nothing in the
deployment path — not `.env.example`, not the Dockerfile's build arguments, not
`build:storefront`, not `compose.prod.yml` — so every image this repository built
served canonicals, a sitemap and a robots.txt naming the `http://localhost:3000`
its reader falls back to, and the build reported success. The stand-in this file's
previous entry describes was exactly that finding, parked; it has retired.
A7 is what stops the repair being four files that gained a line. The run points
the instance's storefront-address variables at an origin that is deliberately not
the compiled-in one, lets that value reach `next build` through the `.env` the
command itself wrote, and then reads `<link rel="canonical">` out of the page the
configured boot served. A canonical carrying the fallback is a red criterion that
names the fallback; a page with no canonical is `unmeasured`, never a pass.
THE ADDRESS DERIVATION CHANGED UNDER BOTH A6 AND A7, AND THE SIX EARLIER STATES
ARE UNCHANGED BECAUSE OF IT. Which variables name the backend was read off the
*shape* of a value in `.env.example` — an absolute http(s) URL — which was right
only while that file declared no address but the backend's. Supplying the public
origin there makes it wrong: A6 would have pointed the shop's canonical origin at
the API host, and `endora new storefront` would have told a client, in a file they
own outright, that it 'names the backend this storefront talks to'. The question is
now asked of the declaration's own `addressOf` field, which says what each value
is rather than what it looks like.
SINCE 2026-09-07 THE RECORD IS ALSO REPRODUCIBLE, WHICH IT HAD NEVER BEEN. Every
state above was measured on a developer's machine, and A5 had not passed once in
CI — 163 runs of `acceptance:storefront-scaffold` since it landed, of which zero
succeeded. The difference was one variable this criterion inherited and handed on:
NODE_ENV=development, which the job sets job-wide and correctly, for the *backend*
it boots. Next loads the copy's `.env` and does not override a variable the process
already carries, so the harness's environment configured the instance over the top
of what `endora new storefront` wrote. The criterion now withholds every name the
copy's own declaration says its process reads, and the report says which. Nothing
in this record moved, and that is the finding: a recorded state nobody could
reproduce is a recorded state that says less than it looks like.

registry.why: The route now runs — the three packages published at `0.7.0`, and job 43527 on master resolved all three of them from the registry (`A3 PASS ... resolving 3 published ranges`), which retires this entry's previous reason that they were unpublished at `0.0.0`. It is still `unrun` because no *honest* run of it exists: the one measurement, job 43527, was made while the criterion handed the instance the harness's own `NODE_ENV=development`, so its `A5 fail` and `A6 unmeasured` describe that defect rather than this supply route, and recording them would assert that a scaffolded storefront is expected not to build. This tree cannot produce a better one — `ENDORA_NPM_REGISTRY` and `ENDORA_NPM_TOKEN` are protected CI variables and `projects/:id/variables` answers 403 to the credential available here, while `resolveMode` correctly refuses a registry with no token rather than making an anonymous attempt. The seven states are therefore recorded by the first master pipeline after the environment repair lands: it drifts, names every state it measured, and that run is the author. Do not fill this in from the tarball mode's block — `A3 pass` means a different thing under each.

history.what: A6 gained a discrimination probe, and the harness started configuring the instance with the variables the instance declares
history.detail: The six states are unchanged. `boot()` set PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL, which is the backend's own variable and which the storefront reads nowhere, so every A6 measured the compiled-in `http://localhost:3001` fallback: 200 when the run's backend sat there, 500 when it sat anywhere else. Measured on master at http://127.0.0.1:3101 — `A6 FAIL ... answered / with 500` — against a scaffolded instance that serves 200 the moment BACKEND_BASE_URL names the same backend. The names now come off the instance's own `.env.example` through the derivation `endora new storefront` prints in its next steps, they reach `next build` as well as `next start` because Next inlines a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable at build time, and a second boot against an address nothing listens on has to fail before the first is read as a pass.

history.what: the criterion landed with the command (F7 scaffold half), all six green
history.detail: A1 the copy names nothing above its own directory; A2 no `workspace:` range survives; A3 `pnpm install` outside the checkout from three packed tarballs, pinned through `pnpm.overrides` because page-builder-core's own dependency on contracts is equally unpublished; A4 every @endora-commerce/* package resolves outside the checkout; A5 `next build`; A6 `next start` answered / with 200 against a running backend.

history.what: the record became per supply route; `tarball` keeps its six measured states, `registry` arrives unrun
history.detail: Feature 104 § 1.6. The criterion gained a second mode that installs from a registry rather than from packed tarballs, selected by ENDORA_NPM_REGISTRY. The tarball mode is unchanged in every respect — same six assertions, same states, still the default — and its block is the previous `assertions` object moved under it. Nothing about the two-way drift rule changed; what changed is which block a run is compared against.

history.what: the run supplies the five inputs the command requires; the six states are unchanged
history.detail: Measured on this branch against a backend at http://127.0.0.1:3101: `mode=tarball pass=6 fail=0 unmeasured=0 of 6`, with the command reporting `[inputs] resolved: total=5 flags=5 env-file=0 prompted=0 generated=0 defaulted=0`. On master the same invocation exited 2 — `endora: 5 required inputs are not set, and this run cannot ask for them` — with every assertion unrun. Nothing about the six assertions changed and nothing about the two-way drift rule changed; what changed is that the criterion now hands the command the inputs it declares required, deriving both the population and the values from the storefront's own files. `backend/test/unit/acceptance/storefront-scaffold-assertions.test.ts` holds the derivation to that declaration in the fast suite, so the next required input added without a value the criterion can reach fails in seconds rather than after an install, a build and two boots.

history.what: A7 arrives, and it is measured rather than predicted: the served canonical names the origin the instance was built with
history.detail: `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` was declared required by `storefront/environment-inputs.mjs` and supplied by nothing in the deployment path, so every image this repository built served canonicals, a sitemap and a robots.txt naming `http://localhost:3000` while the build reported success. Measured on this branch against a backend at http://127.0.0.1:3711: `mode=tarball pass=7 fail=0 unmeasured=0 of 7`, with A7 reading `<link rel="canonical" href="https://shop.acceptance.invalid">` out of the page the configured boot served. The value reaches that build through the `.env` the command wrote from the flag the run supplied — declared, resolved, written, inlined, served — rather than through a variable the harness exported over the top of it, which is what makes A7 a measurement of the chain and not of one export. The origin is deliberately not the compiled-in one, so the pass cannot be the fallback's; a canonical carrying the fallback is a red criterion that names it. Separately and by hand, on the reference storefront built with `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://shop.example.com`: `/` served that canonical, `/sitemap.xml` those `<loc>`s and `/robots.txt` `Sitemap: https://shop.example.com/sitemap.xml` — the third being the surface no container environment could ever have repaired, because Next prerenders it into the image.

history.what: the seven tarball states did not move, and for the first time a CI run can reproduce them: the criterion stopped handing the instance this harness's environment; the `registry` block keeps `unrun` and loses a reason that had gone false
history.detail: A5 had never once passed in CI. 163 runs of `acceptance:storefront-scaffold` since it landed on 2026-09-03 — 124 canceled, 27 failed, 12 skipped, 0 succeeded — and the earliest that reached A5 at all (job 40410, master 10a0ab9d, 2026-09-04) failed with the same sentence as the latest (job 43544, MR !1479, ca43192c5): `<Html> should not be imported outside of pages/_document`, from the prerender of `/404`. It is not a regression of any branch and it was never about the packages the instance installs. Reproduced here by exporting NODE_ENV=development and varying nothing else — same checkout, same install, byte-identical message down to the chunk offset `2303.js:6:1351` — and isolated to Next itself: a four-file `app/` with no dependency of this repository in it fails identically under `next build`, and passes with NODE_ENV unset, `production` or `test`. The mechanism, measured rather than inferred: `next build` inlines `process.env.NODE_ENV` as `"production"` into the server bundle it emits, so the emitted `_document.js` and `_error.js` name `pages.runtime.prod`, while the render worker reads the real NODE_ENV and loads `pages.runtime.dev` — two module instances of Next's vendored pages runtime, two `React.createContext()` calls, and an `<Html>` consuming the context the other one provides. The variable reached that build because this criterion inherited `process.env` into the instance's install, build and boot, and the job sets NODE_ENV=development job-wide for the *backend* it boots, which is correct and stays: with NODE_ENV=production that backend refuses its own boot over an unset SESSION_COOKIE_SECRET. So the repair is at the seam, not in the storefront, not in the scaffold's output and not in a dependency range: a process run inside the instance is given the instance's environment, with every name the copy's own `environment-inputs.mjs` says its process reads withheld unless this run deliberately supplied it. Measured on this branch with NODE_ENV=development exported and a backend at http://127.0.0.1:3711 — the CI shape exactly — `mode=tarball pass=7 fail=0 unmeasured=0 of 7`, `the run agrees with the recorded expectation`, with the report naming `withheld NODE_ENV`. The population is the declaration and never a list, so it tightens by itself when the storefront declares another variable; `backend/test/unit/acceptance/storefront-scaffold-assertions.test.ts` holds the rule in the fast suite and asserts that the reference storefront still declares NODE_ENV, which is what stops the coverage lapsing in silence. The supply route was never the variable and it is worth writing down which measurement says so: the same failure occurred under *both*. Job 43527 (master, registry) resolved three published ranges from the real registry and failed A5; job 43544 (!1479, tarball) installed three packed files and failed A5 with the identical message. Two dependency-resolution paths, one build failure — so the scaffolded instance having no lockfile, which is real and is filed as a finding of its own, is not what breaks this build. The `registry` block's `why` is rewritten in the same breath because it claimed the opposite: it said the packages were unpublished at `0.0.0`, which 43527's own A3 refutes. It stays `unrun` because the only run of that route measured this defect, and this tree cannot make a better one — the registry and its token are protected variables, `projects/:id/variables` is 403 here, and `resolveMode` rightly refuses a registry with no token instead of attempting an anonymous install. The first master pipeline after this merge is the author of that block: it will drift, and the drift line names every state it measured.
